PROTEST OF CLEAN ENERGY ADVOCATES AND COMMUNITY 
ORGANIZATIONS 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”)1, Clean Energy Advocates2  and 
Community Organizations3 respectfully submit this protest in response to the October 2, 2026 
filing of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) in the above-captioned 
docket, which proposes revisions to MISO’s Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating 
Reserve Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish a Large Load Addition Resource Study (“LARS”) 
process.4 For the reasons explained below, the Commission should reject the LARS proposal. 
 
 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.211. 
2 Clean Energy Advocates are Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council, and Sustainable 
FERC Project, Clean Grid Alliance, Clean Wisconsin, and Fresh Energy. 
3 Community Organizations are Community Collaboration on Climate Change and Michigan 
Environmental Justice Coalition. 
4 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Large Load Addition Resource Study Process, Docket 
No. ER27-25-000 (Oct. 2, 2026), Accession No. 20261002-5074 (“LARS Filing”). Citations to 
the “Transmittal Letter” are to the transmittal letter accompanying the LARS Filing. Citations to 
the “Drake Testimony” are to the Prepared Direct Testimony of Christina Drake, Director, 
Generation Interconnection, MISO, submitted as Tab C to the LARS Filing.

3 
I. 
Introduction 
As the Commission has recognized, integrated planning processes can help ensure that 
generation and transmission can be arranged to supply nearby large customers reliably, at lower 
cost, and with faster engineering study processes, ultimately resulting in more just and 
reasonable rates without harming other existing or future customers or suppliers. Better load and 
generation interconnection processes are clearly needed. MISO’s LARS proposal does not 
achieve that end, nor does it improve other interconnection processes. Instead of improving the 
coordination of generation and transmission planning, MISO’s LARS proposal is a new, 
permanent parallel interconnection study process that will shift costs from large loads to other 
existing and future transmission customers and resource owners, create and worsen reliability 
concerns, and allow for unchecked and harmful anti-competitive discrimination. The 
Commission should reject LARS because it is not just and reasonable and is unduly 
discriminatory or, in the alternative, issue a deficiency letter requiring MISO to demonstrate how 
LARS can be made just and reasonable.  
II. 
Background 
A. Large Load Growth and Interconnection 
MISO estimates that annual load growth will be 1 to 3 percent per year from 2025 
through 2044.5 MISO integrates new generation and load through separate processes on different 
schedules.6 New generation enters either through MISO’s cluster-based Definitive Planning 
Phase (“DPP”) or its temporary, serialized Expedited Resource Addition Study (“ERAS”). The 
DPP operates on a 365-day timeline and ERAS operates quarterly. New load is accounted for 
 
5 Transmittal Letter at 2-4. 
6 Drake Testimony at 3–4.

4 
through the MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”) or the Expedited Project Review 
(“EPR”). Where MTEP operates on an 18-month cycle, EPR provides approval in roughly 90 
days. MISO acknowledges that “large loads have overtaken the EPR process.”7 The 89 EPR 
requests approved in MTEP26 accounted for roughly 54 percent of the approximately $14.7 
billion of transmission investment approved in that cycle.8 
A generator may be treated as an alternative to a transmission solution only once that 
generator has a signed interconnection agreement (“GIA”).9 This poses a timing problem. A 
large load whose transmission solution depends on a new generator cannot obtain MTEP 
approval until the generator has completed the DPP or ERAS interconnection queues. MISO 
describes this “timing problem” as the problem the LARS parallel study process is designed to 
solve.10 
B. The Show Cause Order 
On June 18, 2026, the Commission instituted a proceeding under section 206 of the 
Federal Power Act (“the Act” or “FPA”), preliminarily finding that MISO’s Tariff “appears to be 
unjust and unreasonable because it lacks provisions that address, with sufficient clarity and 
consistency, how MISO and/or the Transmission Owners will timely study . . . the provision of 
transmission service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads.”11 The Commission directed 
MISO to show cause why the Tariff remains just and reasonable without provisions addressing

(a) application, study, and ongoing operational requirements for Eligible Customers serving large 
loads; (b) transparency concerning large-load-driven Network Upgrade costs and a pro forma 
cost recovery agreement “to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers”; (c) 
co-location arrangements; (d) transmission services for co-located, behind-the-meter, and 
flexible large loads; and (e) “the rates, terms, and conditions of service applicable to 
interconnection customers serving electrically proximate large load or co-located load.”12 Three 
parts of the Show Cause Order bear directly on LARS: study procedures, cost shifting, and 
proximate loads. 
1. Study procedures for large loads 
The Commission found that the Tariff lacks “sufficiently clear and consistent provisions 
regarding the study process” for large loads, pointing to the “ad hoc study process” reflected in 
Transmission Owner study agreements “not reflected in MISO’s Tariff,” and identified the 
elements such provisions should contain. These include: 
(1) A definition of large load. 
(2) A rolling application process with non-refundable fees, escalating readiness 
requirements, and disclosure of duplicative requests. 
(3) Study procedures that account for large-load behavior and flexibility. 
(4) Evaluations of alternative transmission technologies “in all instances,” with a 
written demonstration whenever traditional Network Upgrades are selected 
instead. 
(5) A 60-to-90-day study deadline. 
(6) Ongoing operational requirements. 
 
12 Show Cause Order at P 33.

6 
(7) Pro forma transmission service agreement provisions.13 
2. Cost shifting 
The Commission found that the Tariff “appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it 
lacks adequate mechanisms to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers,” 
and identified two remedies. First, public posting of the Network Upgrades needed to serve large 
loads and their costs.14 Second, a pro forma cost recovery agreement requiring the Eligible 
Customer to make “a minimum contribution toward the transmission owner’s transmission 
revenue requirement,” sized to the megawatts of service requested and secured by credit support, 
so that large-load-driven costs are not “paid by other transmission customers that neither caused 
the need for nor benefit commensurately from those Network Upgrades.”15 
3. Generation serving electrically proximate load 
The Commission defined an “electrically proximate large load” as one “sufficiently 
electrically close to the interconnection customer’s requested point of interconnection” that the 
combined impact of generator and load “will be effectively the same as if they were located at 
the same substation (e.g., large load that is located no more than two substations away from the 
generating facility),” and invited revisions “appropriately tailored to MISO’s transmission 
system.”16 It found that MISO’s Tariff is deficient because it lacks a study process or 
interconnection service that reflects “an interconnection customer’s commitment in an 
interconnection agreement to limit the generating facility’s output” while serving such a load.17

Referencing SPP’s High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”) 
process, the Commission stated that such a generator’s interconnection service “should be of an 
interim nature until the interconnection customer obtains” Energy Resource Interconnection 
Service (“ERIS”) or Network Resource Interconnection Service (“NRIS”), and noted that 
MISO’s system “may warrant consideration of a more limited definition of electrically 
proximate.”18 The Commission directed that any responsive filing to the Show Cause Order 
address whether such generators would participate in MISO’s energy, ancillary services, and 
capacity markets, with what restrictions, and how they would be accredited.19 
The Commission “strongly encourage[d]” MISO to address these directives through 
filings under section 205, but specified that any such filing “should also explain which of the 
Commission’s above directives their filing addresses and how it resolves them.”20 
C. The LARS Proposal 
On October 2, 2026, MISO filed proposed revisions to Attachment X (the Generator 
Interconnection Procedures, or “GIP”), Appendices 1 and 6 to Attachment X, and Attachment FF 
to establish the Large Load Addition Resource Study, with a requested effective date of 
December 2, 2026 and a first study period in the first quarter of 2027.21 MISO described LARS 
as “expedited review of the addition of 200 MW or greater loads together with new generation 
resources that are electrically proximate to those loads,” conducted in a parallel study process 
lasting up to 120 days that builds on EPR and ERAS.22 Unlike ERAS, however, LARS “will be a 
permanent MISO study process.”23

19 Id. at P 127.

LARS creates at least two major changes to how generation interconnection and 
transmission planning function in MISO. First, LARS creates an exception to the EPR 
requirement described above in which a generator can be considered an alternative transmission 
solution only after it has a GIA. Under MISO’s proposed process, a generator that has submitted 
a valid LARS application and holds a five-year or longer contract (e.g., Power Purchase 
Agreement or similar off-take agreement) with the large load “may be considered as an 
alternative transmission solution” in the load study even though it does not have a GIA.24 
Second, the proposed process creates a new, 120-day serial generator interconnection track 
outside of the DPP and ERAS, through which the paired generator receives NRIS under a new 
form of agreement called the Large Load Generator Interconnection Agreement (“LLGIA”).25 
MISO presents LARS as responsive to the Show Cause Order’s electrically proximate directive 
and resource adequacy concerns, and as independent of “[t]he cost shifting issues raised in the 
Commission’s Show Cause Order,” which “will be addressed in future filings.”26 
Four entities drive the LARS process. Only the entity that procures transmission service 
for a large load may initiate and submit a LARS Application.27 This entity is called a “LARS 
Associated Transmission Customer,” which MISO states is often a Load Serving Entity 
(“LSE”).28 MISO’s proposal does not set any criteria, timelines, or disclosure obligations on a 
LARS Associated Transmission Customer’s decision whether to sponsor a particular generator 
and load. A generator-load pair, however, has no path into LARS without such sponsorship.29

Second, the Interconnection Customer develops a generating facility, demonstrates that it will 
provide energy to the LARS Associated Load, and signs the LLGIA.30 Third, the Transmission 
Owner coordinates with the Interconnection Customer to identify a “definitive Point of 
Interconnection,” supplies the initial transmission solutions that are evaluated in the load study, 
and constructs the necessary Network Upgrades.31 Finally, the “LARS Associated Load” is 
defined as a single load of at least 200 MW at one Point of Withdrawal.32 
 
A LARS Application must include an executed agreement with a term of at least five 
years, “evidencing that the output of the Generating Facility . . . shall be used to provide energy 
to the LARS Associated Load.”33 The Interconnection Customer must request NRIS of at least 
200 MW and no more than 150 percent of the LARS Associated Load’s expected peak demand, 
demonstrate 100 percent site control, and pay an application fee of $250,000 and an entry 
milestone of $30,000 per MW.34 Aside from the 150 percent cap, nothing requires the paired 
generation to be sized to any particular share of the load’s demand. Nor do the eligibility criteria 
require any demonstration of a reliability or resource adequacy need. The Point of 
Interconnection must be in the same Local Resource Zone (“LRZ”) as the load’s Point of 
Withdrawal.35 A LARS Associated Load may be served by more than one Interconnection 
Customer, though MISO will accept only ten LARS Applications total per study period.36 The 
generator’s commercial operation date and the load’s full in-service date must fall within three

acknowledges that it “does not have a requirement that loads bring generation,” and characterizes 
LARS as “an incentive for Load to bring Generation.”38 
MISO will accept applications on a rolling, “serial ‘first-come, first-served’” basis and 
study up to ten generation/load pairs in each of the three study periods per year.39 On the 
generation side, each generator is studied “individually in a serial fashion” in its own model.40 
The LARS base model includes existing generators, generators with executed GIAs, and 
approved MTEP and EPR projects, but excludes DPP projects without an executed GIA.41 On 
the load side, the study is “built upon MISO’s existing EPR process.”42 All ten load-generation 
pairs are represented together in a single MTEP-based model, the Transmission Owners’ initial 
solutions are evaluated, and MISO establishes a planning-level solution.43 Although the load-
generation pair must be located in the same LRZ, “MISO will look at the full impacts of the 
generation/load pair on MISO’s Transmission System using the same study criteria and 
processes applicable to NRIS evaluations of other Interconnection Requests.”44 If there is an 
overallocation because transmission capacity is ultimately found to have been allocated to both a 
LARS generator and a DPP generator, the resulting constraint “will be formalized in a future 
MTEP project,”45 “neither will be required to pay additional costs,”46 and the MTEP project’s

With respect to cost allocation, MISO allocates mitigations to the Baseline Reliability 
Project (“BRP”) or “Other” project types except for mitigation violations observed in the 
generation study, which are assigned to the Interconnection Customer as Generator 
Interconnection Project (“GIP”) upgrades.48 BRP and Other upgrades are constructed by the 
Transmission Owner and the costs are recovered through transmission rates under the existing 
provisions of Attachment FF rather than funded by the Interconnection Customer. According to 
MISO, these costs will most likely be allocated to “the load within the transmission pricing zone 
where the transmission upgrade is required.”49 
LARS generators receive full NRIS, allowing them to “qualify as a Network Resource for 
capacity and resource adequacy needs” and to “participate in the Planning Reserve Auction.”50 
The LLGIA does not require output to be tied to the load except insofar as the generator cannot 
inject until some portion of the load is in service.51 Once the load is fully in service, the LLGIA 
does not limit the generator’s output in any way.52 While the generator’s output is not limited by 
its paired load, the generator and load must remain contractually paired for at least fifteen years 
after the load begins taking service.53 MISO justifies the fifteen-year term as “a standard duration 
for large load contracts” and as sufficient “to deter entities from invoking the needs of a specific

D. The Stakeholder Process 
MISO developed LARS in eleven weeks. It first presented the concept to its Large Load 
Working Group (“LLWG”) on July 16, 2026.55 After presenting revisions at different meetings, 
MISO presented final language on September 23 and filed on October 2.56 
Stakeholders raised, and MISO declined to address, several of the concerns presented in 
this protest. The Environmental Sector objected to the Transmission Customer’s gatekeeping 
role, to the LRZ-wide scope of the pairing requirement, and to LARS’s failure to meet the Show 
Cause Order’s electrically proximate standard, and asked that generators and loads be jointly 
liable for upgrade costs if a pairing ends early. Energy Futures Group presented the Generator 
and Load Interconnection Process (“GALIP”), which would study large loads and their 
generation together within the DPP, with full cost-causation-based allocation of upgrade costs 
and both firm and non-firm service options for load.57 MISO declined to pursue GALIP, stating 
that it “does not believe in a ‘one size fits all’ approach to interconnection” and that GALIP 
“aimed to shoehorn a parallel generation/load study process into the existing DPP process.”58

III. 
Arguments 
A. LARS creates a cost shift from large loads and their generation to other 
customers 
It is a long-standing principle of Commission ratemaking that “all approved rates reflect 
to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay them,” and that 
compliance is measured “by comparing the costs assessed against a party to the burdens imposed 
or benefits drawn by that party.”59 In the Show Cause Order, the Commission preliminarily 
found that MISO’s Tariff violates that principle because it “lacks adequate mechanisms to 
mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers” when large loads drive network 
upgrades.60 LARS does not supply those mechanisms. By MISO’s own account, LARS adopts 
no cost allocation methodology, and “[t]he cost shifting issues raised in the Commission’s Show 
Cause Order will be addressed in future filings.”61  
Instead, LARS builds cost shifting into the process in four ways. First, it assigns the 
network upgrades that a generator-load pair requires to the transmission pricing zone rather than 
to the pair. Second, it studies LARS generators in models that exclude the DPP queue, and 
resolves the resulting double-allocation of transmission capacity through MTEP projects paid for 
by zonal load and through curtailment of DPP generators that paid for their own upgrades. Third, 
it allows either half of a pair to leave the system after fifteen years and the generator to fail at any 
time, leaving zonal load to pay for whatever transmission must then be built. Fourth, it defers the 
cost recovery agreement, financial security, and transparency measures the Commission 
identified as necessary. The Commission should reject LARS or, at a minimum, decline to make

KN Energy, Inc. v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992)); Ill. Commerce Comm’n v. 
FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir. 2009).

it effective until the cost provisions MISO has promised are filed, accepted if consistent with the 
Order to Show Cause principles, and incorporated into the LARS Tariff provisions. 
1. LARS assigns upgrade costs to the pricing zone 
As explained above, LARS sorts network upgrades identified in its load and generation 
studies into three categories: violations in only the load study, violations in only the generation 
study, and violations in both studies. Violations that occur only in the load study or in both the 
load and generation studies are assigned the BRP or Other project types and their costs are 
allocated to all loads in the Transmission Owner’s pricing zone. Only when a violation occurs in 
the generation study alone will MISO assign the costs of the mitigations to the Interconnection 
Customer as a GIP upgrade.62 MISO calls this a “cost allocation hierarchy—transitioning from 
GIP to BRP when appropriate.”63 This hierarchy represents impermissible cost shifts.  
When the costs of mitigation are assigned to BRP or Other project types, those costs are 
allocated to the Transmission Owner in whose pricing zone the project is located. Those costs are 
then recovered through the Transmission Owner’s rates, paid for by every transmission customer 
in the zone. MISO explains that the costs will fall on “the load within the transmission pricing 
zone where the transmission upgrade is required.”64 In contrast, when the same generator 
interconnects through the DPP, the Interconnection Customer funds the Network Upgrades its 
interconnection requires. LARS, therefore, takes a category of costs usually assigned to 
generators and assigns them to existing load. It is not as though the beneficiaries are unknown or 
diffuse. Rather, the beneficiaries are simply the generator and the large load, for which the 
generator is the “alternative transmission solution.”65 MISO has failed to show how the LBA or

LRZ suddenly benefit from the needed upgrades simply because violations show up in the load 
and the generation studies. And in none of these situations is the cost assigned directly to the 
large load that is driving the need for the upgrades. This kind of cost shifting is exactly the sort 
of thing the Commission found unjust and unreasonable in the Show Cause Order. 
LARS is likely to shift the cumulative upgrades needed to support the transmission 
system, because of the serialized LARS study process. Each LARS generator is studied 
“individually in a serial fashion” in its own model.66 Unlike a DPP cluster study, which identifies 
the upgrades a group of generators needs together and allocates their costs among the cluster, the 
LARS generation study never captures the combined effect of the ten generators and loads in a 
study period, let alone of the thirty pairs that may enter LARS each year. In fact, constraints that 
emerge from the cumulative injection of LARS generators or cumulative impacts of LARS large 
loads are most likely to appear in a load study where all ten pairs are studied together. In that 
case, however, as explained above, those mitigations will be classified as BRP or Other. 
Otherwise, the problems will reveal themselves in a later MTEP study. Either way, costs will be 
allocated not to the load-generation pair, but to all load in the zone. 
The pricing zone that pays for upgrades caused by LARS projects may not even be the 
LBA in which the LARS Associated Load takes service. While load-generation pairs must be in 
the same LRZ, MISO studies “the full impacts of the generation/load pair on MISO’s 
Transmission system” without confining the study to that zone.67 A single LRZ can span 
multiple LBAs, Transmission Owner pricing zones, and states. Because MISO declined to limit 
the generation/load pairs to a single LBA or to a set number of substations, the result is that 
customers of one Transmission Owner, in one state, can be assigned the cost of upgrades

required because a data center in another state chose to contract with a generator sited near them. 
The state regulator responsible for protecting those customers has no jurisdiction over the load 
that caused the cost, and the retail large load tariffs states are adopting to protect their ratepayers 
cannot reach a load in another state.68 This is textbook cost shifting, which the Commission has 
recently noted as a concern in the large load context.69 
Transmission upgrade costs associated with LARS generation should not be assigned to 
load generally, because both the driver and the beneficiaries of the upgrade are a specific 
generator-load pair.70 The NRIS service for a LARS Interconnection Customer hinges on the 
consumption of the LARS associated load. MISO acknowledges this tight connection by 
terminating the LLGIA, and sending the generator back to the DPP for new interconnection 
service if the load leaves or shrinks within fifteen years.71 A generator whose interconnection 
service is contingent on one load’s consumption is not a system resource whose upgrades benefit 
the zone. 
MISO insists that the LARS Associated Transmission Customer “remains responsible for 
the identified BRPs and Other assigned projects even if such LARS Associated Load does not 
commence service.”72 Yet the Tariff contains no mechanism through which a Transmission 
Customer pays for the BRP or an Other project. A Transmission Customer’s only

responsible for, the costs incurred to provide them with the requested transmission service, 
including the costs of any needed Network Upgrades.”73 Rather than responding to the 
Commission’s call to fill this gap in cost recovery agreements, MISO merely states that the “cost

Commission preliminarily found unjust and unreasonable because they lack “adequate 
mechanisms to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers.”75 
MISO states that “a pro forma cost shifting agreement will need to be executed and new

Associated Transmission Customer to execute any such agreement, post any security for the BRP 
and Other upgrades assigned to the zone, or take any defined transmission service. The only 
party that posts security in LARS is the generator, and only for the GIP upgrades that LARS

2. LARS shifts costs to interconnection customers in the DPP 
LARS shifts costs to interconnection customers in the DPP, to the disadvantage of 
generators in the DPP compared to those related to LARS projects. In the DPP, MISO models 
the system headroom by assuming that all higher-queued generating facilities will enter 
operation.78 By contrast, in LARS, MISO proposes to model only DPP projects with a signed 
GIA.79 These differing approaches risk MISO allocating transmission headroom twice.80 Rather 
than reconcile the double-allocation, MISO proposes that “[b]oth [projects] will be allowed to 
proceed, and neither will be required to pay additional costs due to the overallocation.”81 Failing 
to coordinate DPP and LARS shifts costs onto DPP customers. 
LARS generators are studied as though the DPP queue does not exist. They are assigned 
none of the upgrades that their injections require in combination with the queued projects ahead 
of them. Those upgrades are left to the DPP customers, who are assigned them on the assumption 
that the headroom in their models would still exist when they reach commercial operation. When 
LARS and DPP generators both come online and the system cannot deliver to both, the result is a 
reliability gap. This leads to unplanned curtailments and degraded operating conditions, which 
will result in instances where the DPP customer would have been able to export energy and

receive market payments, but for the LARS customer causing unmitigated congestion. While 
interconnection customers do not have a right to any particular system topology, a decrease in 
available headroom and degraded operating conditions represent cost shifts to generators in the 
DPP, because that same headroom is instead being allocated to LARS projects. 
In the long term, MISO proposes that the constraints caused by the double-allocation of 
headroom will be “formalized in a future MTEP project”82 whose cost falls on “the load within 
the transmission pricing zone.”83 Reliance on future MTEP projects, however, is both 
insufficient and too late. MISO’s reliance on later MTEP cycles will not cure the reliability gap 
caused by the double-allocation.84 LARS projects, not having been studied with the advanced 
Phase 3 DPP interconnection projects reaching commercial operation in the same time frame, 
may cause costly reliability upgrades in that future MTEP cycle, yet those costs will now become 
shifted to other transmission customers and market participants.85 While this presents its own set 
of cost-shifting concerns, it also does not address the fact that these further upgrades identified in 
later MTEP cycles might take years to construct. During this time, the LARS generator would

served process. Each request under LARS is studied “individually and in a serial fashion based 
on their submission date.”135 MISO argues that this serial process “avoids the dependence on the 
overall cluster of generating facilities moving forward.”136 
Unlike other expedited interconnection processes approved by the Commission, LARS is 
permanent. For example, the Commission accepted PJM’s Reliability Resource Initiative as a 
one-time departure, and Commissioners Rosner and Phillips wrote that they would not have 
found it just and reasonable otherwise.137 While the Commission accepted MISO’s revised 
ERAS proposal, ERAS includes a sunset date and puts a cap on the number of participants.

MISO asks the Commission to allow a permanent serial side-queue it has allowed only as a 
temporary and bounded exception in recent decisions. 
LARS is also counter to the need for certainty that the Commission insisted on in Order 
No. 2023.138 LARS reduces certainty for DPP participants in at least two ways. First, as shown 
above, LARS generators are studied without the DPP queue and DPP customers are studied 
without LARS generators, so that the upgrade assignments in both processes rest on models 
MISO concedes are separate and distinct.139 Second, LARS has no restudy process and MISO 
will tender LLGIAs before affected system results are available, which it concedes is “necessary 
to maintain the accelerated speed of the LARS process.”140 MISO seeks to trade certainty for 
speed for a privileged few data centers and their paired generation. 
Order Nos. 2003 and 2023 were also designed to accomplish an open access purpose of 
ensuring non-discriminatory access to the transmission system. Here too, MISO’s LARS 
proposal does not accomplish the purposes of the Commission’s interconnection orders. As 
discussed supra, LARS does not meet the goals of enabling open access to the transmission 
system because it places access to the LARS interconnection process under the gatekeeping 
control of self-interested vertically integrated utilities. It grants preferential treatment to 
generators interconnecting through LARS compared to generators seeking to interconnect 
through the DPP process.  
Additionally, the Commission’s interconnection orders were designed to streamline 
interconnection processes and create a standard, unified interconnection process. By creating a

simplifying goal.  
Finally, Order No. 2023 was designed to increase the speed of interconnection for new 
generation interconnection requests. While LARS might fast track a limited set of privileged 
interconnection requests, the creation of a new interconnection queue will put competing 
pressures on MISO’s staff and compute time to process standard DPP requests. And while MISO 
stated that LARS deposits will fund “additional tools, staffing, and process enhancements” rather 
than drawing on DPP resources,141 MISO still undermines the purpose of Order No. 2023 to the 
extent DPP is not receiving these marginal additional resources to speed DPP timelines.142 
D. MISO’s LARS proposal is not responsive to Commission direction regarding 
“electrically proximate” generation and load from the Show Cause Order 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission found that MISO’s Tariff “appears to be 
unjust and unreasonable” because it did not contain provisions allowing an interconnection 
customer to serve “an electrically proximate large load.”143 Rather than directly responding to the 
Commission’s Order, MISO invents a new expansive definition of “proximate” in an attempt to 
demonstrate that its proposal is responsive to the Commission’s Order. It is not. 
The Commission defined electrically proximate load as a large load “that is sufficiently 
electrically close to the interconnection customer’s requested point of interconnection, such that 
the impact on the transmission system of the combination of the generating facility and the load, 
with the exception of the transmission facilities between the two, will be effectively the same as 
if they were located at the same substation.”144 MISO chose not to conform to this definition and

MISO argues that this new definition is appropriate because the Commission stated that it 
would “consider proposed revisions to this definition to ‘ensure it is appropriately tailored to 
MISO’s transmission system.’”146 However, as MISO itself concedes, its definition of proximate 
is not grounded in the unique structure of its transmission system, and instead MISO simply “did 
not want to limit the pairing of generation with associated load to a specific number of 
substations because that is likely too geographically narrow and could limit how MISO may 
optimize common transmission solutions.”147 As such, even MISO’s novel definition of 
proximate is inconsistent with the flexibility afforded by the Commission on this issue. 
Additionally, MISO justifies this choice by arguing that tying LARS Associated Load to 
Local Resource Zones “avoids price separation between the paired generation and LARS 
Associated Load.”148 However, Local Resource Zones do not always align with transmission

will not easily be able to ensure that transmission costs associated with large load additions are 
assigned to that load. Local Resource Zones are intended to reflect capacity and reliability needs, 
not transmission cost recovery. MISO intentionally separates these constructs because they

E. LARS threatens reliability and efficient planning 
LARS would be at least the fifth separate path onto the MISO transmission system, 
alongside the DPP, ERAS, the pending Zero-Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement 
(“ZGIA”) process, and EPR for load. A sixth, the Large Load Project Review (“LLPR”) is 
currently under development.150 MISO’s addition of another parallel interconnection process 
takes the region further away from efficient transmission planning. MISO’s statement that any 
constraints that are not addressed in the LARS study due to overallocation would be reconciled 
in the MTEP process does not promise that these solutions would be minimal upgrades.151 It 
promises only that they would be reconciled through the MTEP process. There is a risk under 
MISO’s current proposal that unresolved reliability contingencies identified in a subsequent 
MTEP process could require mitigation through backbone upgrades or other high-cost solutions 
resulting from the cumulative impacts of LARS and other interconnection requests, the costs of 
which non-LARS transmission customers would ultimately have to pay. Due to the permanent 
nature of MISO’s LARS proposal, there is a risk that non-LARS transmission customers could 
be permanently disadvantaged by the process and bear the costs of transmission investments 
needed to resolve issues caused, at least in part, by a LARS request, or series of interconnection 
requests. Each new path to interconnection takes MISO further from efficient planning.

151 Transmittal Letter at 13.

40 
1. Parallel independent studies produce unreliable results and reliability risks 
Interconnection studies assign network upgrades on the basis of cumulative impacts. By 
putting some generators in one model and other generators in another, MISO cannot capture 
those impacts. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation’s (“NERC”) model 
validation guidance states that future-year planning cases “should contain the same component 
representations as the most recently validated model, unless there is a specific reason for the data 
to be different,” and should represent “the cumulative planned changes to the system” through 
the period studied.152 By excluding the DPP, LARS does the opposite of NERC’s procedures. 
Neither set of studies sees the other until MTEP, which is after LLGIAs have been executed and 
DPP customers have been assigned their upgrades. 
The consequences of this mutual blindness of the models are not limited to the cost shifts 
described above. A constraint that appears only when the two sets of projects are combined 
might be a contingency for which no mitigation was identified and no upgrade was built, leaving 
real-time operators without the reconfiguration options the planning process assumed. In the 
worst case, cascading blackouts could result. A more moderate negative outcome might be load 
shed as the only tool available to manage unstudied conditions. MISO does not appear to 
describe the dispatch and case assumptions for the LARS load study. MTEP-based load studies 
and DPP interconnection studies in MISO are built on different cases and different dispatch 
assumptions. Without an explanation of which assumptions LARS will use, the Commission has 
no basis to find that a load study built upon MISO’s existing EPR process will identify the 
constraints that a DPP study of the same generator would identify.

Siloing also creates questions around generator retirement. If a LARS generator retires 
within the fifteen-year pairing period, the Tariff says the load may go through MTEP, but it does 
not say whether the Attachment Y retirement study and the MTEP restudy of the load occur in 
sequence or in parallel, or who bears the upgrades needed to keep serving a load whose MTEP 
approval rested on a generator that no longer exists.153 Once future MTEP cycles combine 
generators from the serial and cluster processes into a single model, a withdrawal or retirement in 
either process can require restudy in the others. MISO has not addressed these interactions. 
2. Siloed, expedited processes are already driving MISO’s largest 
transmission investments outside regional planning 
MISO acknowledges that “large loads have overtaken the EPR process.”154 In MTEP26, 
roughly 54 percent of the $14.7 billion of approved transmission investments originated in EPR, 
as did eight of the ten largest Appendix A projects, representing approximately $6 billion.155 
Transmission additions to the MISO grid of this magnitude will have a dramatic impact on 
power flows throughout MISO’s system, and continuing the analysis of large load needs in an 
isolated process like that outlined in LARS risks harmful impacts to other transmission 
customers. By MISO’s admission in its LARS filing, the EPR process has become increasingly 
challenging due to the volume and type of facilities proposed through this process. Take, for 
instance, the proposed 500 kV Smalling–El Dorado and 500 kV West Fork–St. Landry lines and 
the 230/500 kV West Fork substation facility evaluated through MISO’s EPR process. These two 
transmission lines span over 200 miles across Louisiana and Arkansas, and the 230/500 kV

3. Integrated planning processes are available and MISO should adopt them 
There are viable alternatives to siloed transmission planning, which is inefficient and 
costly. In March, the Commission accepted SPP’s Consolidated Planning Process (“CPP”), 
which, in Commissioner Rosner’s description, “eliminat[es] the silos between the transmission 
planning process and the generator interconnection process” by “synthesizing and streamlining 
them into one recurring three-year planning cycle” that “recognizes that generation and load 
share one transmission system, and plans for both of their needs holistically.”160 Commissioner 
Rosner “strongly encourage[d] other transmission providers to take note of the innovative 
approach the CPP promises, and to consider developing similar integrated solutions tailored to 
meet the pressing needs within their own footprints.”161 Commissioner Rosner noted that SPP 
expected to deliver interconnection agreements within nine to ten months of the close of its 
application window, to cut study costs by millions of dollars, and to avoid more than $100 
million in duplicative transmission costs each planning cycle.162 PJM, responding to its own 
show cause order, has proposed to “[c]onsolidate generation and merchant transmission 
interconnection along with long-term firm and large load transmission service studies into a 
singular 12-month process.”163 Transmission planning becomes more efficient the more future 
transmission needs can be considered together in the planning process. This is one of the reasons

MISO’s disagreement with the GALIP proposal reveals its interconnection ethos: “MISO 
offers different interconnection products to meet different needs.”168 This is problematic for three 
reasons. First, meeting every new need with a new, siloed interconnection process (as MISO has 
done with ERAS, the ZGIA, now LARS, and soon the LLPR) significantly increases network 
upgrade costs and the risk of MISO missing the combined system impacts of all of these parallel 
processes. Second, multiple interconnection paths increase the risk of bias and subjective 
assignment of preferential treatment, as discussed above. Third, interconnection studies are 
performed in sequential order where each stage builds on the models, assumptions, and data of 
the previous one. Parallel interconnection paths, particularly ones like LARS where the impact is 
not constrained to a single point of interconnection, are inherently flawed. Since the physics of 
load and generation interconnection are inextricably tied, MISO’s approach of parallel studies 
will fail to provide a complete view of transmission needs and system demands for LARS 
resources.  
IV. 
Conclusion 
For the foregoing reasons, the Commission should reject all portions of MISO’s LARS 
proposal and direct MISO to engage with stakeholders to advance a different proposal.  
Alternatively, Clean Energy Advocates and Community Organizations request that the 
Commission issue a deficiency letter directing MISO to address the issues in this protest. Either 
course of action should focus on an integration of planning processes that does not undermine 
the DPP queue or shift costs to DPP customers.
